PSI-10.summary: The investigation ran spherical diffusion flames in drop towers and aboard the International Space Station. It varied dilution, flow rate, pressure and flow direction for ethylene and methane flames. It aimed to find soot-inception limits, measure flame properties, and find extinction limits, including radiative or kinetic extinction.
PSI-10.habitatRelevance: The text frames its impact around terrestrial combustors and does not address crewed habitats directly. It gives microgravity evidence on soot formation and flame extinction that a designer could consult, but it does not say how that applies to habitat materials or fire response.
quotes: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests in drop towers and aboard the International Space Station.
Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of N2, and pressure for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 flames.

PSI-20.summary: The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) uses a porous gas burner on the ISS to mimic burning of condensed fuels in still microgravity air. It varies oxygen level, pressure and diluent to map burning conditions and extinction limits. It tests whether steady or quasi-steady burning can exist as a function of material properties.
PSI-20.habitatRelevance: The text reports that flames kept burning without air flow in elevated-oxygen atmospheres being considered for future spacecraft, while flames in normal atmosphere self-extinguished in a short time. The results are described as preliminary, and ignition limit tests were not proposed for microgravity.
quotes: Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow
While BRE’s results are still preliminary

PSI-21.summary: ACME CLD Flame studied weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene in microgravity, varying fuel dilution and velocity. It measured flame shape, lift-off height, temperature, extinction limits and soot behavior to give benchmark data for testing computational flame and soot models.
PSI-21.habitatRelevance: The text links understanding of diffusion flame extinction to fire suppression and describes soot formation, but it reports no habitat-specific fire tests. Its evidence is benchmark data for improving models, not direct habitat fire-safety results.
sensors: flame chemiluminesence of OH* and CH*
quotes: an understanding of those factors that affect flame extinction in diffusion flames is critical in the suppression of fires
Flame temperatures in non-sooting regions will be measured using thin-filament pyrometry.

PSI-22.summary: This investigation studied how electric fields change small laminar gas-fueled diffusion flames in microgravity, where buoyancy does not mask the effect. It measured the link between field voltage and ion current through the flame, the flame's response to field changes, soot formation, and near-limit lifted flames.
PSI-22.habitatRelevance: The text says the work is not conducted for space applications, though findings might aid future space combustion devices such as solid waste processing. It gives no direct evidence on fire ignition, detection or suppression in a crewed habitat.
quotes: The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications
Dilution levels were varied to explore a range of combustion dynamics, from highly stable to near-extinction flames.
There were thermopile detectors to measure flame radiant emissions.

PSI-23.summary: ACME s-Flame plans microgravity experiments in which gaseous fuel and diluent mixtures flow through a spherical porous burner to form nearly spherical, one-dimensional diffusion flames, soot-free and sooty. It aims to characterize flame structure, find extinction limits, and look for pulsating instabilities, then compare results with detailed simulations.
PSI-23.habitatRelevance: The work gives evidence on how diffusion flames are sustained, extinguished and produce soot in a buoyancy-free environment, which informs understanding of flame extinction and soot formation. The text frames it as fundamental combustion science with gaseous fuels, not as a test of habitat materials or fire-suppression systems.
quotes: Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits
mixtures of various gaseous fuels and diluents will be issued into an oxidizing environment through a spherical porous burner and ignited

PSI-25.summary: BASS-II burned solid fuel samples in a small wind tunnel inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox on the International Space Station. It varied airflow and oxygen level to study ignition, flame growth, spread and extinction, and to compare microgravity burning with the normal-gravity flammability test.
PSI-25.habitatRelevance: The evidence supports fire detection and suppression system design and material selection by giving data and model validation on how solid materials burn in low-velocity flows in microgravity. It covers the tested fuels, geometries, flows and oxygen levels only, not all habitat conditions.
quotes: Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.
Flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent flow.

PSI-26.summary: BASS burned fabric, Nomex and Ultem samples, plus spheres and cylinders, in a small flow duct on the ISS to see how materials burn in microgravity over long test times. It also tested how well an inert gaseous extinguishing agent puts out flames across materials, geometries, preheating and flow.
PSI-26.habitatRelevance: The work targets a gap between the standard normal-gravity material flammability test and real material behavior in microgravity, and links nitrogen suppression to current and planned extinguishment techniques. The text does not state that any material or agent has been shown adequate for a habitat.
quotes: Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.
Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects.

PSI-39.summary: The Cool Flames Investigation burned fuel droplets in microgravity inside the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus. It looked at n-dodecane, farnesane and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures, including helium dilution. It aimed to learn how cool flames behave, how droplet size and pressure relate to extinction, and what soot forms.
PSI-39.habitatRelevance: The text says the work will support the design of safer spacecraft systems by refining knowledge of combustion in microgravity. The evidence is about liquid hydrocarbon fuel droplets, so it does not directly address habitat materials, and no detection or suppression tests are described.
quotes: Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction
support the design of safer spacecraft systems by refining knowledge of combustion in microgravity environments

PSI-47.summary: DAFT and DAFT-2 checked whether a modified TSI P-Trak particle counter could measure aerosols accurately in microgravity, to reduce risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment. The modified instrument counted Arizona Red Dust aerosol held in Mylar bags, and its readings were compared with a DustTrak control.
PSI-47.habitatRelevance: The work supports building more reliable and sensitive smoke and fire detection for the International Space Station and future spacecraft, since aerosol counters must work without gravity. The text describes an instrument feasibility test, not a test of fire behavior or suppression.
quotes: DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity.
This research will impact the development of novel fire and smoke detection systems for the International Space Station and future spacecrafts.

PSI-60.summary: This ground investigation combined image analysis and soot modeling to explain why soot formation differs between normal gravity and microgravity flames. It used Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) images to derive flame temperatures and soot volume fractions, then compared them with simulations of two burner configurations.
PSI-60.habitatRelevance: The work aims to improve predictive models of soot formation and flame structure in microgravity, which could inform smoke production estimates and fire detection and suppression design. It is a ground-based analysis of existing data and models, so the text does not show direct habitat-scale fire test results.
quotes: improve understanding of soot formation, oxidation, radiative re-absorption, and aggregate growth in heavily sooting flames
the results support safer fire detection, suppression, and cleaner combustion technologies critical for long-duration missions

PSI-62.summary: This investigation developed and tested a flamelet generated manifold modeling method for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Simulations of BASS and BASS-II geometries were compared against experimental imagery, processed with two-color tomography, to see whether the model reproduces flame behavior and the flammability zone.
PSI-62.habitatRelevance: The work aims to give habitat designers a predictive tool for screening spacecraft materials' flammability limits and for hazard assessment in confined habitats. The text describes model development and comparison with experiments, and does not report completed validation results.
quotes: to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials
enabling 3D reconstructions of soot and temperature fields for direct comparison to model predictions

PSI-68.summary: FLEX-2 studied burning of single and bi-component liquid fuel droplets in microgravity across varied pressure, oxygen level, fuel type and droplet size. It aimed to extend FLEX-1 results, examine flame extinction and soot formation, and give benchmark data for validating combustion models.
PSI-68.habitatRelevance: The text addresses fuel droplet combustion for engines and combustors, not habitat fire scenarios, so it gives only indirect evidence on ignition, extinction and soot behavior in microgravity. It does not describe habitat materials, detection or suppression.
sensors: pressure and temperature data of the chamber environment
quotes: Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries.
Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics.
Monitor combustions and track flame evolution using high speed photography.

PSI-69.summary: FLEX burned relatively large liquid fuel droplets in microgravity to map flammability limits, test how gaseous suppressants change those limits, and support predictive models. Tests varied ambient pressure, oxygen fraction and droplet size to find the Limiting Oxygen Index, with some tests adding a slow convective flow.
PSI-69.habitatRelevance: The work gives evidence on how liquid-fuel flames extinguish and how suppressants affect flammability limits without buoyancy, which can inform habitat fire protocols. The text covers droplet burning only, so other fuels, materials and habitat-scale fires remain untested here.
quotes: A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .

PSI-98.summary: SAFFIRE-I ignited a large piece of cotton and fiberglass fabric inside a flow duct on an uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle after it left the ISS. It aimed to learn how fast a large fire grows in low gravity and how low-gravity flammability limits compare with NASA's normal-gravity screening test.
PSI-98.habitatRelevance: The text presents this as a way to study a realistic, large-scale fire without risk to a crew, addressing a lack of microgravity data for spacecraft fire safety design. It reports no results, so the text does not show what the findings mean for habitat design.
quotes: determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity
There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures.

PSI-99.summary: SAFFIRE-II set out to learn how quickly a large fire grows in low gravity and how low-gravity flammability limits compare with NASA's normal gravity material screening test. It burned a card of material samples in a flow duct aboard an uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle after it left the ISS.
PSI-99.habitatRelevance: The work gives spacecraft designers large-scale low-gravity fire data that they have lacked, and helps check NASA's material selection criteria. The text does not report results or say which conditions or materials remain untested for a crewed habitat.
quotes: determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity
There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures.

PSI-100.summary: SAFFIRE-III ran fire experiments on an uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle after it left the ISS. It burned SIBAL samples in concurrent or opposed flow to learn how fast a large fire grows in low gravity and how low-gravity flammability limits compare with NASA's normal gravity screening test.
PSI-100.habitatRelevance: The text says spacecraft fire safety designs rely on terrestrial fire data despite uncertainty, and this large-scale test aims to supply low-gravity data for designers. It reports no results, so what it shows about habitat fire behavior is not stated.
quotes: determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity
There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures.

PSI-101.summary: SAME-R was a reflight of the SAME smoke experiment. It aimed to measure how large liquid smoke particles become in low gravity and to link droplet size to how the smoke was generated and transported. It used a new foam test material, broader test conditions and a new instrument.
PSI-101.habitatRelevance: The work supports fire detection for future long-duration spacecraft by providing reduced-gravity smoke data against which detectors can be evaluated. The text says smoke particle size may change detector response and possibly cause some detectors not to alarm.
quotes: The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors
The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated.

PSI-102.summary: SAME studied smoke made by overheated spacecraft materials in the Glovebox to learn how large liquid smoke droplets grow in low gravity. It also tested how two smoke detectors respond, and aimed to build a numerical code predicting droplet growth from pyrolysis rate, vapor properties and flow.
PSI-102.habitatRelevance: The evidence gives reduced-gravity baseline data on smoke particle size and detector response, which can be used to judge whether existing smoke detection technology is adequate for spacecraft. The text indicates some detectors might not alarm if smoke particles differ in low gravity, but that is a hypothesis in the text, not a result.
quotes: The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated.

The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.

PSI-106.summary: SLICE studied how laminar diffusion flames are structured and held in place in microgravity. A fan-driven duct with exchangeable burner tubes burned several fuels, including nitrogen-diluted mixtures, under coflow air. A camera and flow and temperature sensors recorded the flames to compare them with normal gravity and to validate models.
PSI-106.habitatRelevance: The work gives evidence on how small, steady flames behave and stay stabilized in microgravity, plus soot formation and radiative heat loss, which may inform habitat fire understanding. The text tests controlled laboratory burner flames, not spacecraft materials or habitat-scale fires, and does not assess detection or suppression.
sensors: sensors to measure flow rates and temperature
quotes: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity.
A high resolution camera captured still images while sensor data was overlaid on these images.

PSI-107.summary: SPICE burned small gas-jet flames in a co-flow of air inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox on the ISS, with analogous ground tests. It aimed to find the smoke point, where a flame starts emitting soot, and how burner size, co-flow velocity and fuel type affect flame length and sooting.
PSI-107.habitatRelevance: The work addresses soot production and flame behavior without buoyancy, which informs how fires might behave in a spacecraft. The text says it will help design safer spacecraft environments, but it covers small laminar jet flames, not materials fires, detection or suppression.
quotes: Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity.
Fuel flow rates were adjusted to identify the smoke point, marked by the flame's transition to emitting soot.

PSI-115.summary: This investigation used numerical simulation, not a flight fire test, to compare how pyrolysis smoke particles form and grow in microgravity versus Earth gravity. It modeled dibutyl-phthalate particles from a heated sample at low cross-flow speeds, drawing on geometry similar to the SAME experiments, to find what drives the differences.
PSI-115.habitatRelevance: The work suggests gravity changes smoke particle formation and growth, which bears on how smoke detectors are designed for crewed habitats. The text reports modeling only, with no measured detector performance or fire tests.
quotes: to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke
This would directly lead to better smoke detection devices

PSI-117.summary: This ground study used flight data from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to build a 3-D computer model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity. It simulated how imposed heating, droplet-drift convection, or both change ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction, and mapped stability conditions.
PSI-117.habitatRelevance: The text says the models could improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame and extinction behavior in microgravity. The evidence is simulation of fuel droplets checked against FLEX data, so it does not directly address materials or fires in a habitat.
quotes: Potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame/extinction behavior in microgravity

PSI-142.summary: This grant used data from the FLEX space station flame extinguishment experiments, plus new simulations and ground-based ozone-sensitized counterflow flame experiments, to study when hot flames turn into cool flames. It examined how oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion and convection affect cool flame extinction and flammability limits.
PSI-142.habitatRelevance: The work is fundamental and mostly computational, so it informs understanding of near-limit flame behavior, including in microgravity where long residence times are possible. The text does not describe habitat materials, fire detection or suppression testing.
quotes: Obtaining a fundamental understanding of the warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments
The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames.

PSI-159.summary: ACME CFI-G plans ISS flight tests of spherical diffusion flames to find the conditions under which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane and n-pentane. It varies fuels, dilution, flow rate, pressure and flow direction, and supports the tests with CFD simulations and chemical kinetics work.
PSI-159.habitatRelevance: The text frames this work around cool flame chemistry and engine efficiency, not habitat fire safety, so it gives no direct evidence on fire hazards in a crewed habitat. It does show that cool flames can be sustained and studied in microgravity, and that they can transition to hot flames or go out when flow changes.
quotes: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station.
Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.
